opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Divine Mercy Sunday is the Sunday after Easter, established by Pope John Paul II based on the message given to Saint Faustina Kowalska.

It exists to make one point clear: the Resurrection is not just that Christ rose—it is what He does next.

The Gospel shows Jesus Christ appearing to His disciples. He shows His wounds, breathes on them the Holy Spirit, and gives them authority to forgive sins. That is direct. His suffering becomes the source of mercy, and that mercy is now active.

But not everyone received it the same way.

Thomas, called Didymus, was not there the first time. When he was told, he did not believe. He said plainly that unless he saw the wounds himself, he would not accept it. When Jesus returned, He did not reject Thomas. He showed him exactly what he asked for—the wounds—and met him where he was.

At the same time, Scripture is honest about where we actually live.

As written in First Epistle of Peter: *although you have not seen Him, you love Him; even though you do not see Him now, you believe in Him and rejoice with an indescribable and glorious joy, as you attain the goal of your faith, the salvation of your souls.*

That is not describing a perfect life. It is describing a real one.

Most people are not standing in clear outcomes. They are in the middle—where things are uncertain, where efforts don’t always turn into results, where something gets close and then falls through. You keep moving, but the repetition starts to wear on you.

This is where it becomes easy to think something is wrong with you or your faith.

But the issue is not belief. It is fatigue under delay.

You can love God, trust Him, and still feel tired of starting over. You can believe fully and still look at your life and see very little that reflects what you hoped would have happened by now.

Divine Mercy speaks into that situation directly.

You are not received by God based on visible outcomes.
You are not behind because your life has not come together yet.

Mercy means God already knows your situation—and still moves toward you, not away from you.

At the same time, faith is not passive.

The same reality that says you are fully received also calls you to continue—to act, to move, to stay engaged in your life even when results are not guaranteed.

So both are true at once:

You are not required to prove yourself to God.
But you are still called to live, not withdraw.

That tension does not go away.

You believe, even without seeing.
You continue, even when things are unclear.

And in that, whether it is visible yet or not, something real is taking place—the movement toward the goal of your faith.

Not later.

Now.
